---
title: "The model"
---

The model is an agent-based stress test of 67 euro-area significant institutions.
A shock weakens banks' capital and triggers depositor runs; each bank then meets its
liquidity need by choosing among four funding channels — outright **sales**,
**unsecured** borrowing, private **repo**, and **central-bank credit** — and those
choices feed back into asset prices and into each other through a multi-week cascade.

The visual below shows the mechanism the paper is about: **how banks move through the
capital–liquidity plane as the cascade unfolds, and how the collateral framework
changes that path.**

## The capital–liquidity plane

Every bank lives in a plane with two axes: its **CET1 capital ratio** (horizontal)
and its **liquidity coverage ratio** (vertical). Stress pushes a bank through this
plane, and where it goes determines whether it stabilises or spirals. Two thresholds
matter:

- **CET1 = 10%** — below this a bank's depositors start to run, and the runs intensify
  as capital falls further, reaching full intensity at **CET1 = 8.5%**.
- **LCR = 100%** — the regulatory liquidity floor.

### A typical bank under stress

The illustration below traces a *stylised* bank through the plane as the cascade
advances — step through it with the slider. Under **sales only**, meeting outflows by
fire-selling erodes both capital and liquidity: the bank drifts down and left, crosses
the LCR floor, enters the run zone, and spirals. Under the **full framework**, the same
bank pledges collateral instead — liquidity holds up, capital is preserved, and it
stays clear of the run threshold.

```{ojs}
mockSales = [
  {step:0, cet1:14.0, lcr:150}, {step:1, cet1:13.0, lcr:128}, {step:2, cet1:12.0, lcr:110},
  {step:3, cet1:11.0, lcr:98},  {step:4, cet1:9.6, lcr:84},   {step:5, cet1:7.8, lcr:68},
  {step:6, cet1:5.6, lcr:54},   {step:7, cet1:3.8, lcr:44}
]
mockFramework = [
  {step:0, cet1:14.0, lcr:150}, {step:1, cet1:13.6, lcr:146}, {step:2, cet1:13.3, lcr:141},
  {step:3, cet1:13.1, lcr:139}, {step:4, cet1:12.9, lcr:138}, {step:5, cet1:12.8, lcr:137},
  {step:6, cet1:12.8, lcr:137}, {step:7, cet1:12.7, lcr:136}
]
viewof mstep = Inputs.range([0, 7], {step: 1, value: 7, label: "Cascade step"})
```

```{ojs}
sSales = mockSales.filter(d => d.step <= mstep)
sFrame = mockFramework.filter(d => d.step <= mstep)
posSales = mockSales.filter(d => d.step === mstep)
posFrame = mockFramework.filter(d => d.step === mstep)
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  width: 720, height: 460, grid: true,
  x: {domain: [2, 15], label: "CET1 ratio (%)"},
  y: {domain: [30, 160], label: "LCR (%)"},
  marks: [
    // threshold regions on the capital axis
    Plot.rectX([{}], {x1: 2, x2: 8.5, fill: "#d7301f", fillOpacity: 0.10}),
    Plot.rectX([{}], {x1: 8.5, x2: 10, fill: "#fc8d59", fillOpacity: 0.12}),
    Plot.ruleX([8.5], {stroke: "#d7301f", strokeDasharray: "3,3"}),
    Plot.ruleX([10], {stroke: "#e34a33", strokeDasharray: "3,3"}),
    Plot.ruleY([100], {stroke: "#2166ac", strokeDasharray: "3,3"}),
    Plot.text([{x: 9.25, y: 34}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: ["runs intensify"], fontSize: 10, fill: "#b30000"}),
    Plot.text([{x: 5.2, y: 34}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: ["full run intensity"], fontSize: 10, fill: "#b30000"}),
    Plot.text([{x: 14.6, y: 104}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: ["LCR floor"], fontSize: 10, fill: "#2166ac", textAnchor: "end"}),
    // trajectories
    Plot.line(sSales, {x: "cet1", y: "lcr", stroke: "#d7301f", strokeWidth: 2, marker: "circle"}),
    Plot.line(sFrame, {x: "cet1", y: "lcr", stroke: "#1a9850", strokeWidth: 2, marker: "circle"}),
    Plot.dot(posSales, {x: "cet1", y: "lcr", r: 7, fill: "#d7301f"}),
    Plot.dot(posFrame, {x: "cet1", y: "lcr", r: 7, fill: "#1a9850"}),
    Plot.text(posSales, {x: "cet1", y: "lcr", text: ["Sales only"], dy: -14, fill: "#d7301f", fontWeight: "bold"}),
    Plot.text(posFrame, {x: "cet1", y: "lcr", text: ["Full framework"], dy: -14, fill: "#1a9850", fontWeight: "bold"})
  ]
})
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
This trajectory is **illustrative** — a stylised single bank drawn to show the
mechanism and the thresholds. The thresholds themselves are the model's actual values:
runs begin at 10% CET1, reach full intensity at 8.5%, and the LCR floor is 100%.
:::

## Collateral-conditional liquidity

The heart of the model is a simple idea: **the same asset is worth a different amount
of liquidity depending on how you try to raise cash against it.** A bank can *sell* an
asset (and take a price discount), *repo* it (and take a private haircut), or *pledge*
it at the *central bank* (and take the Eurosystem haircut). An asset that is nearly
cash-good in one channel can be useless in another.

### Why the channels differ

Pick an asset below. The bars show, illustratively, how much usable liquidity €1 of
that asset yields in each channel — and the note explains why.

```{ojs}
archetypes = [
  {asset: "Government bond", sales: 0.90, repo: 0.98, cb: 0.99,
   why: "Deep market and a tiny haircut: liquid in every channel, and best of all at the central bank."},
  {asset: "Covered bond", sales: 0.85, repo: 0.94, cb: 0.93,
   why: "Marketable and eligible: sellable at a modest discount, and pledgeable in both repo and at the central bank."},
  {asset: "Corporate bond", sales: 0.72, repo: 0.80, cb: 0.85,
   why: "Thinner market and larger haircuts, but still usable in all three channels."},
  {asset: "Bank loan (credit claim)", sales: 0.00, repo: 0.00, cb: 0.65,
   why: "Non-marketable: it cannot be sold or repo'd at all. Only the central bank accepts it — at a haircut — which is exactly what the collateral framework controls."},
  {asset: "Equity", sales: 0.60, repo: 0.00, cb: 0.00,
   why: "Sellable at a discount, but ineligible as collateral anywhere: no repo, no central-bank credit."}
]
viewof pick = Inputs.select(archetypes, {label: "Asset", format: d => d.asset})
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  height: 220, width: 640, marginLeft: 120,
  x: {domain: [0, 1], label: "Usable liquidity per €1", tickFormat: "%"},
  y: {label: null},
  color: {legend: false},
  marks: [
    Plot.barX([
      {channel: "Sell", v: pick.sales},
      {channel: "Repo", v: pick.repo},
      {channel: "Central bank", v: pick.cb}
    ], {y: "channel", x: "v", fill: "channel", sort: {y: null}}),
    Plot.text([
      {channel: "Sell", v: pick.sales},
      {channel: "Repo", v: pick.repo},
      {channel: "Central bank", v: pick.cb}
    ], {y: "channel", x: "v", text: d => d.v === 0 ? "unusable" : (d.v * 100).toFixed(0) + "¢",
        dx: 6, textAnchor: "start"}),
    Plot.ruleX([0])
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
md`**${pick.asset}.** ${pick.why}`
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
These five archetypes use rounded, illustrative haircuts to convey the mechanism; the
next chart shows the actual schedule.
:::

### The realised schedule

Averaged over the actual Eurosystem eligibility and haircut schedule (and the LCH repo
schedule and the sales-discount calibration), here is the liquidity value of €1 in each
channel by asset category. The pattern the model turns on is stark: **loans and credit
claims are essentially unusable except at the central bank**, while government paper is
usable everywhere.

```{ojs}
chl = FileAttachment("../data/channel_liquidity.csv").csv({typed: true})
chLabel = ({sales: "Sell", repo: "Repo", cb: "Central bank"})
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  width: 900, height: 380, marginLeft: 160,
  x: {domain: [0, 1], label: "Usable liquidity per €1", tickFormat: "%"},
  y: {label: null},
  fy: {label: null},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["sales", "repo", "cb"],
          tickFormat: c => chLabel[c], label: "Channel"},
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(chl, {
      x: "liquidity_value", y: "channel", fill: "channel", fy: "category",
      sort: {y: null}
    }),
    Plot.ruleX([0])
  ]
})
```
